description: We are a team of enthusiasts—comprising amateur writers and professionals from diverse fields. We have come together to create an educational research game for schoolchildren—one that offers an engaging world of interactive elements and encourages the exploration of forgotten NASA equipment.
summary:
We are a team of enthusiasts who have created an educational exploration game for schoolchildren. This game invites them to explore the fascinating world of forgotten NASA space equipment. 
NASA’s NEAR was the first spacecraft to enter orbit around the asteroid 433 Eros, and also the first to land on it in 2001.
This game is designed for an age range of 6+ to infinity.
School teachers can use it as a quick warm-up activity, and later provide the children with more detailed information about the NEAR Shoemaker spacecraft itself, its mission, and its achievements. Thus, this game has excellent potential for success in any educational setting.
details:
Basic game rules:

The game has 3-sections.

1) You must carefully fly from Earth to the asteroid 433 Eros. During the flight, the player collects test tubes and dodges comets approaching the spacecraft.

While playing, the child learns brief facts about the NEAR Shoemaker spacecraft, which encounters another asteroid—253 Mathilde—along its path and captures many different photographs.

The player also learns that Earth's gravity captured the NEAR Shoemaker spacecraft and flung it further—much like a slingshot—which helped save fuel.

Shortly thereafter, an engine on the spacecraft misfired, forcing scientists to adjust its trajectory and perform a loop; this extended the flight time to the asteroid by one year.

2) In this section, as players approach the asteroid, they learn that the NEAR spacecraft captured 160,000 images and collected a vast amount of data on craters, boulders, the magnetic field, and rock formations.

3) The player must concentrate and monitor the speed and fuel levels in the craft to ensure a successful landing on the asteroid.

Educators in schools can use this game as a short warm-up activity, and subsequently explain the spacecraft, its journey, and its mission to the children in greater detail. The game is easy, accessible, and understandable.

The following programming languages ​​and software were used:

Languages: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (vanilla, no frameworks or game engines)

Browser APIs: Canvas 2D (all graphics are drawn in code), Web Audio API (sound effects generated in code), Pointer/Touch events (mobile controls)

Fonts: Google Fonts (Baloo 2, Nunito)

Hosting: GitHub Pages

Analytics: GoatCounter (cookieless)

Tools: JetBrains IDE with Junie (AI assistant), VS Code with Claude Code (AI assistant), Git/GitHub

Cover images: generated from the game's own drawing code with a Bash script, headless Google Chrome and Python.
